Gini Index

Source: R/gini_index.R
gini_index.Rd

Estimates the Gini index of inequality from a sample of nonnegative values such as incomes, wealth, sales, or citation counts. The Gini index is 0 when every unit has the same amount and approaches 1 when a single unit holds everything.

Usage

gini_index(x, na.rm = TRUE)

Arguments

x

A numeric vector of nonnegative values with at least two observations, not all zero.

na.rm

Should missing values be removed before the calculation? Default TRUE. With na.rm = FALSE a missing value is an error.

Value

A single number between 0 and 1, the estimated Gini index.

Details

The population Gini index is \(G = \Delta / (2\mu)\), where \(\Delta = E|X_1 - X_2|\) is Gini's mean difference (see gini_mean_diff) and \(\mu\) is the mean. It is defined for nonnegative data with a positive mean. The estimate returned is $$G_n = \frac{\hat{\Delta}_n}{2 \bar{X}_n},$$ the sample Gini mean difference (the average of \(|x_i - x_j|\) over all pairs) divided by twice the sample mean, which is the estimator used in the sequential procedure of Chattopadhyay and De (2016) that seq_aipe_gini implements. Because the average is over pairs of distinct observations, \(G_n\) equals \(n / (n - 1)\) times the "plug in" Gini index that some software reports; the two agree as the sample grows. The estimate does not change when every value is multiplied by the same positive constant.

References

Chattopadhyay, B., & De, S. K. (2016). Estimation of Gini index within pre-specified error bound. Econometrics, 4(3), 30. doi:10.3390/econometrics4030030

See also

seq_aipe_gini for the sequential confidence interval; gini_mean_diff.

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Francis Bilson Darku fbilsond@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Annual salaries (in thousands of dollars) of ten employees of a firm.
salary <- c(28, 31, 35, 38, 42, 47, 55, 64, 90, 170)
gini_index(salary)
#> [1] 0.3503704

# Equal salaries give 0; the index does not depend on the currency unit.
gini_index(rep(50, 10))
#> [1] 0
gini_index(1000 * salary)
#> [1] 0.3503704
